title: Maximum XOR of Any Two Elements
statement: A hardware team encodes sensor readings as non-negative integers and measures how 'different' two readings are by XOR-ing them: the bigger the XOR, the more their bit patterns disagree. Given a list nums of at least two non-negative integers (each value at most 2^31, list length up to 10^5), return the single integer max(nums[i] ^ nums[j]) over all index pairs with i != j. The same index may not be paired with itself, but equal values at different indices are a valid pair (their XOR is 0). The answer always exists since len(nums) >= 2. An O(n^2) scan of all pairs is too slow at the top of the size range; aim for O(n log MAX) by deciding the answer one bit at a time from the most significant bit down, keeping a set of prefixes masked to the bits decided so far and using the identity a ^ b = c  <=>  a ^ c = b to test whether the current candidate answer with the next bit set is achievable.
hints: Comparing every pair is O(n^2). Could you instead decide, one bit at a time, whether the final answer can have that bit set? Which end of the number should you start from?

Go from the most significant bit down. Maintain 'best' (bits decided so far) and a growing mask; at each bit, collect the set {n & mask for n in nums} and ask whether two prefixes XOR to candidate = best | (1 << bit). The identity a ^ b = c  <=>  a ^ c = b turns that pair question into set lookups.

For each bit from 31 down to 0: extend mask by that bit, build the prefix set, form candidate = best | (1 << bit), and if any prefix p has (p ^ candidate) also in the set, commit best = candidate. Greedily keeping a high bit is always safe because one higher bit outweighs all lower bits combined. Return best.
